title: Mica Tablet Site
summary: In 1849, New York State received a mica plate reportedly found while plowing in Brookhaven. Engraved geometric and other figures make the object unusual, but its exact findspot, age, and cultural interpretation remain uncertain.
map_geometry_source: Broad public orientation point for Fireplace Road/Brookhaven from OSM/Nominatim and Directus text; not the findspot or sacred landscape location.
why_this_matters: Discovered in the sacred "Fire Place" region of Brookhaven where the Unkechaug traditionally rendered whale blubber, this unique inscribed mica tablet features intricate indigenous carvings. Acknowledging the spiritual and practical significance of this landscape illustrates how deeply Native communities intertwined their everyday maritime survival with profound religious reverence for the ocean's resources.
oral_history_content: In a 2017 oral-history interview, Chief Harry Wallace connected Fireplace Neck with whaling, oil rendering, community places, and a wider sacred landscape. His account emphasizes continuing Unkechaug responsibility for ancestors and culturally important belongings in the area.
history_content: An 1849 acquisition note states that Nathan Miller, a Suffolk County assembly member, sent the New York State collection a plate of mica that had been turned up by a plow about two feet below the ground in Brookhaven. The note described geometric and other engraved figures. John A. Strong later discussed the object in his study of Long Island Algonquian history. The surviving documentation does not establish a precise public location or a single interpretation of the engravings.
artifacts_content: The Mica Tablet is both unique in material and content. The triangular-shaped tablet is approximately 7.75 inches long by 6.25 inches at its widest, and 2.5 inches at the narrow end. [1. Lisa Anderson, May 23rd, 1996, pers.com] The images are very difficult to make out, but there appears to be a serpentine or whale-like effigy (sometimes referred to as great horned-serpent [1. David Martine, Email Correspondence 2017]) with several horns on its head in the center of the tablet. Around the edges, there appear to be images of whale tail fins. The image may be a variation of the horned serpent beings found in Iroquois, Cherokee, and Mississippian belief systems. [1. Hudson 1976, pp. 145-46, String 1989] In New Jersey, a wood carving ca 1750 depicts a similar great horned serpent based on a Manitou or spirit carved on the doorway of a Lenape home.
